title: Bostic sight-reads the hard Oliver arrangements
summary: Bostic plays a difficult part cold and outplays the band.

bands.name: T. Holder's Twelve Clouds of Joy

story.theme_name: Growing up and learning music: family, first instruments, teachers
story.community_name: Reading music versus faking and playing by ear

blocks.x: with us?" says, "75 dollars a week." He says, "How much?" So we says, "75 a week." He says, "I'll go." (Laughter.) Shit, he went home and he didn't have nothing but a toothbrush and maybe a couple shirts and things. He went on and carried them on down there. So now, after we go down there the next day, we all get together, we says, "Wonder can this cat read." So now we're wondering because there's a lot of cats in those days that couldn't read at all. And we said, "Wonder can this cat read." So we says, "Well, we got to find out because we done hired him now." So we just playing light things that night in the ballroom. So King Oliver had arrangements, big sheets called "Muleface Blues" and another tune called "Louisiana Bo-Bo." And it was hard, it was very hard. Now, the way we got it, the reed section would go in the corner and we rehearsed for about an hour and the brass would go in the corner and they would rehearse, rhythm section. So then we say, "Let's see if we can put it together." (Laughter.) That's the way we did it. Hell, it took us a long time to learn that tune, man. And we couldn't play it but so fast then because it was tricky, you know. So we says, -- after we skate along -- his solos was fantastic. He was knocking everybody out in the ballroom.

People standing in front of him, listening to him and all this, you know. But he had that funny sound. He always had a bad tone, that nanny in his sound. It was much worse then than it was when he passed.

So we say, -- we didn't call it "Louisiana Bo-Bo," called that. we called it by the number, the director. So now we're going to see. This separates the men from the boys. He didn't even look at it. So we says, -- the third player reached over and said, "You better let me scuffle with this," he said, "because this got a lot of teeth in it." He says, "Am I to play it later?" So he says, "Yeah." He said, "Well, let me play it now. I might as well F it up now. If I'm going to play it, I might as well learn it."

So everybody says this cat must be crazy -- you know, everybody's all ears, you know. So he says, the director says, "Look at it and see what tempo you want it." He says, "Start it off where you been playing it," says, "that's okay." He says, "I'm learning it. I'm learning it." He just still talkin', says, "I'm learning it." So he said, "No, you stomp it off." (inaudible) That's where we made our mistake. Boy, that stomped that thing off and nobody got out of the introduction.

We let him alone after that. That was the honest to God's truth. Then he wrote arrangements the next day and we couldn't play that.
